facts.text: RAND's Driving to Safety report by Kalra and Paddock, report RR-1478-RC, was published in April 2016.
facts.quote: RAND's Driving to Safety report (Kalra and Paddock, RR-1478-RC, April 2016)

facts.text: RAND's Driving to Safety report found that autonomous road vehicles would require hundreds of millions, and sometimes hundreds of billions, of driven miles to demonstrate reliability.
facts.quote: autonomous vehicles "would have to be driven hundreds of millions of miles and sometimes hundreds of billions of miles" to demonstrate reliability

facts.text: RAND's Driving to Safety report estimated that autonomous road vehicles need 275 million failure-free miles to show, at 95% confidence, a fatality rate no worse than the human rate of 1.09 fatalities per 100 million miles.
facts.quote: 275 million failure-free miles to show, at 95% confidence, a fatality rate no worse than the human 1.09 per 100 million miles

facts.text: RAND's Driving to Safety report estimated that autonomous road vehicles need about 11 billion miles to show a 20% improvement in fatality rate with 95% confidence and 80% statistical power.
facts.quote: about 11 billion miles to show a 20% improvement with 95% confidence and 80% power

facts.text: The logic of the RAND argument transfers to off-road machines: field exposure alone cannot demonstrate rare-event performance.
facts.quote: The logic transfers to off-road machines: field exposure alone cannot demonstrate rare-event performance

facts.text: For off-road machines, per-stratum performance claims at low miss rates require simulation volume plus a credibility argument.
facts.quote: per-stratum claims at low miss rates require simulation volume plus a credibility argument

facts.text: The specific mileage numbers in the RAND argument do not transfer to off-road machines because the off-road claim concerns per-encounter detection and intervention, which can be staged and simulated, rather than a fatality rate per mile.
facts.quote: The specific numbers do not transfer, because the off-road claim concerns per-encounter detection and intervention, which can be staged and simulated, not a fatality rate per mile.
